title: What Is Actually Crawling You
abstract: We analysed 385,057 AI-agent requests across twenty websites over eight months. A measurable share of what every GEO tool reports as AI crawler traffic is not an AI crawler at all: credential-path probing is routinely misclassified as legitimate crawling. We also find inconsistent robots.txt compliance among major AI agents, and show that crawler rankings invert depending on which efficiency metric is applied.

title: Verifiable Trust v5 Specification
abstract: An open, decentralized trust layer letting services, organizations and user agents cryptographically verify identity and authorization before a connection is established. Every participant presents verifiable credentials and resolves trust through a governed ecosystem, inverting the internet's default connect-first-verify-later pattern into verify-first-then-connect, for humans, applications and AI agents alike. I contribute to the specification, including the SD-JWT VC credential container.

title: Conformant but Not Compatible: An Interoperability Study of Thirteen Identity Wallets
abstract: Digital identity rests on a promise: a credential issued by one organisation can be held in any wallet and shown to any verifier, none of whom agreed anything in advance. We read the source of thirteen production identity wallets from governments, companies and open-source projects and recorded what each can actually accept. Four of the five intersections are empty. Wallets also anchor trust in incompatible ways: six ship no trust entries at all, and among those combining a built-in list with a fetched one there are five mutually incompatible rules for which wins. We then integrated one shared trust layer into fourteen wallets across two unrelated credential protocols, with six evidenced issue-then-present round trips on physical devices.

title: Trustless Scientific Collaboration: A Minimal Protocol for Decentralized Agent-to-Agent Trust Using DID:key and Verifiable Credentials
abstract: We design a minimal protocol where two previously unknown AI agents establish mutual cryptographic trust using did:key (Ed25519) and W3C Verifiable Credentials, then collaboratively produce a signed scientific artifact. The protocol requires exactly 2 round trips, adds under 2 ms of overhead, and provides a structural guarantee of impersonation detection.
